title: Communication Skills for Professionals
tagline: Listen, write, present, run meetings and speak up so clearly that colleagues, customers and senior leaders act on what you say the first time.
description:
Most workplace problems in Pakistan are not caused by a lack of effort. They are caused by a voice note nobody understood, an e-mail that buried the request, a meeting that ended without a decision or a hard conversation that never happened. This certification turns communication from a soft skill into a practical, repeatable discipline.

- **How communication works and breaks:** the communication model, common barriers, active listening, skilful questioning and the non-verbal signals that carry feelings.
- **Writing that gets read:** plain language, the pyramid principle and bottom line up front, e-mail and WhatsApp etiquette, and short reports that busy readers can act on.
- **Presenting with confidence:** structure, storytelling, clean slides, managing nerves and handling tough questions.
- **Meetings, feedback and difficult conversations:** agendas, facilitation, minutes, giving and receiving feedback with a situation-behaviour-impact approach, and assertive conversations.
- **Influence across cultures and levels:** ethical persuasion, bilingual English and Urdu workplaces, virtual and hybrid teams, and communicating up to senior leaders.

Every session follows one product launch through a realistic Pakistani company and ends with a scored test. The final exam is scenario-heavy and demanding, so practise as you go.
audience: Professionals at any level who want their e-mails, messages and meetings to produce action
New and aspiring team leads who must give feedback, run meetings and handle difficult conversations
Specialists such as engineers, analysts, auditors and doctors who need to explain complex work simply
Managers who brief senior leaders, boards, customers or regulators
Graduates and early-career staff entering bilingual corporate workplaces in Pakistan
outcomes: Diagnose where a message broke down using the communication model and remove common barriers
Listen actively and ask open, probing and closed questions in the right order to uncover real needs
Write e-mails, WhatsApp messages and short reports that lead with the bottom line and use plain language
Plan and deliver a structured, story-led presentation with clean slides and calm handling of questions
Run purposeful meetings, record decisions and actions, and give and receive feedback constructively
Handle difficult conversations assertively and persuade ethically across cultures, languages and levels
Brief senior leaders concisely, escalate early and frame options for a clear decision

quest.name: Operation Clear Signal
quest.premise: Kehkashan Foods is eight weeks from launching Lehar, its new bottled lassi, in Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad. The product is ready. The communication is not: stock goes to the wrong cities, e-mails go unread, meetings go in circles and old rivalries flare up. As the new Launch Communications Lead, you join the war room with your mentor Nasreen. Clear the static stage by stage and bring Lehar safely to launch day.

badge.name: Clear Signal Communicator
badge.description: Awarded to professionals who proved they can listen, write, present, facilitate and influence clearly across teams, cultures and levels.

cast.name: Nasreen Qureshi
cast.role: Director of Corporate Affairs and your mentor

cast.name: Bilal Chaudhry
cast.role: Head of Sales North, based in Lahore

cast.name: Jamshed Mirza
cast.role: Chief Executive Officer of Kehkashan Foods

sessions.title: Signals and Static: How Communication Works, Breaks and Gets Heard
sessions.summary: Learn the communication model, spot the barriers that distort messages, listen actively, ask questions in a deliberate order and read the non-verbal signals that carry feelings, so your instructions land the way you meant them.
objectives: Use the communication model to locate where a message broke down
Identify semantic, psychological, perceptual, physical, cultural and organisational barriers
Apply active listening techniques: paraphrasing, reflecting feelings, clarifying and summarising
Sequence open, probing and closed questions using the questioning funnel and avoid leading questions
Interpret non-verbal and vocal signals carefully, including in Pakistani workplace settings

cards.title: Three thousand stands in the wrong city
cards.setting: Project Lehar war room, Kehkashan Foods head office, Shahrah-e-Faisal, Karachi. Monday, 9:10 a.m. Eight weeks to launch.

lines.text: Welcome to Operation Clear Signal. Your first morning as Launch Communications Lead, and the war room phone has not stopped buzzing.
(voice note, 0:41) Yaar, I said send the promo stands to the USUAL distributors. Twelve of them in Lahore are asking where their stands are! Who is running this launch?
We sent 3,000 stands to the usual list. The Ramadan list. Sukkur, Larkana, Nawabshah. That is what 'usual' means in dispatch.
The new Lehar distributor list was on the shared drive. I mentioned it in the launch group last week. Did nobody open it?
Nobody here lied and nobody was lazy. Everyone did exactly what they understood. That is what makes this interesting.
Your first mission: find where this message broke, and fix the way we give instructions so it cannot happen again. Then go and listen to Bilal properly.

scenes.heading: Sender and encoding
scenes.narration: Every message starts as an idea in the sender's head. The sender encodes it into words, tone, images or numbers. Bilal's idea was the new Lehar list. The word he chose was 'usual'.

scenes.heading: Channel
scenes.narration: The encoded message travels through a channel: a voice note, an e-mail, a meeting, a phone call. Each channel carries some signals well and others badly. A voice note carries emotion but is hard to search later. Important instructions often need two: a conversation for reasons and questions, and a written record for the details.

scenes.heading: Receiver and decoding
scenes.narration: The receiver decodes the message using their own experience. For the dispatch team, 'usual' had meant the Ramadan list for three years. The words arrived intact. The meaning did not.

scenes.heading: Feedback
scenes.narration: Feedback is the receiver's response that shows how the message was understood. Nobody replied 'Do you mean the Ramadan list?' Without feedback, the sender cannot know a mistake has happened until it is too late.

scenes.heading: Noise and context
scenes.narration: Noise is anything that distorts the message: a noisy warehouse, jargon, stress, assumptions. Context, such as relationships, culture and timing, shapes meaning too. Modern models treat both people as sending and receiving at once.

cards.title: The communication loop
cards.caption: A message is only complete when feedback shows the meaning arrived. Noise can enter at every step.

items.label: Sender has an idea
items.detail: The intended meaning, which only exists in the sender's head.

items.label: Encode
items.detail: Choose words, tone, numbers and visuals that fit the receiver.

items.label: Channel
items.detail: Voice note, e-mail, call, meeting or document, each with strengths and limits.

items.label: Decode
items.detail: The receiver interprets the message through their own experience and assumptions.

items.label: Feedback
items.detail: A reply, read-back or question that shows the sender what was understood.

cards.question: Looking at the Lehar stands mix-up through the communication model, where did the message mainly break down?
options: In the channel, because voice notes cannot carry instructions
In encoding and feedback: an ambiguous word was used and nobody checked what it meant
In decoding only, because dispatch should have known about the new list
In noise, because the warehouse was too loud to hear the voice note
cards.explanation: Bilal encoded his idea with an ambiguous word, 'usual', and no feedback loop existed to catch the different meaning. Dispatch decoded it reasonably from their experience, and the voice note was heard clearly, so the channel and physical noise were not the main problem.

cards.title: The barriers that distort messages
cards.body:
A **barrier** is anything that stops the intended meaning arriving. Learn to name them, because each needs a different fix.

- **Semantic:** words with different meanings, jargon, acronyms, ambiguous terms like 'usual' or 'ASAP'.
- **Psychological:** emotions such as anger, fear or stress that block listening.
- **Perceptual:** assumptions, stereotypes and selective attention; we hear what we expect.
- **Physical and technological:** noise, distance, poor signal, dropped calls, load-shedding.
- **Cultural and language:** different norms for directness, hierarchy or English and Urdu fluency.
- **Organisational:** too many layers, rigid hierarchy, unclear roles, silo thinking.
- **Information overload:** so many messages that important ones are missed.

Most real failures combine two or three barriers. Fix the biggest one first.

cards.title: Name the barrier
cards.prompt: Sort each Lehar launch problem into the barrier type that mainly explains it.

items.text: Finance writes 'GM erosion' in a note to the sales team, who don't know what GM stands for
A brief says deliver 'early next week', read as Monday by one team and Wednesday by another
A plant supervisor, still angry after a shouting match, hears only criticism in a neutral request
Sales assume the plant 'always exaggerates' delays, so they ignore a genuine warning
A new hire is too anxious about looking foolish to ask what an instruction means
The Hyderabad call keeps dropping during load-shedding, so key figures are missed
A briefing is given beside a running bottling line where half the words are lost
An urgent file is shared in a format that will not open on field staff phones

cards.title: Active listening: hearing the meaning, not just the words

scenes.heading: Attend
scenes.narration: Active listening starts with full attention. Phone face down, body turned towards the speaker, and no rehearsing your reply while they are still talking.

scenes.heading: Paraphrase
scenes.narration: Paraphrasing means restating the content in your own words: 'So the twelve Lahore distributors were promised stands by Friday, and none have arrived.' It proves you understood the facts.

scenes.heading: Reflect the feeling
scenes.narration: Reflecting names the emotion you notice: 'You sound embarrassed in front of your distributors.' People calm down faster once their feeling has been acknowledged.

scenes.heading: Clarify
scenes.narration: Clarifying asks about anything vague: 'When you say they are threatening to drop us, is that all twelve or one or two?' It removes guesswork before you act.

scenes.heading: Summarise
scenes.narration: Summarising pulls a longer conversation together at the end: the main facts, the feelings and what happens next. It also gives the speaker a chance to correct you.

cards.title: Five levels of listening
cards.caption: Most of us drift between the lower levels during a busy day. Aim to climb when the conversation matters.

items.label: Empathic listening
items.detail: Understanding the other person's facts, feelings and point of view from their side.

items.label: Active listening
items.detail: Paraphrasing, reflecting, clarifying and summarising to confirm meaning.

items.label: Attentive listening
items.detail: Paying real attention to the words, but not yet checking understanding.

items.label: Selective listening
items.detail: Hearing only the parts that interest you or confirm what you already think.

items.label: Pretend listening
items.detail: Nodding and saying 'haan ji' while thinking about something else.

cards.title: Which technique is this?
cards.prompt: Match each listening response to the technique it uses.

pairs.right: 'So the stands are needed by Friday because the distributors' shelf contracts start on Saturday.'
'It sounds as if you feel let down by head office.'
'When you say ‘quickly’, do you mean today or this week?'
'Let me pull this together: three issues, two are urgent, and you need an answer from Tariq by 5 p.m.'
A nod, 'hmm', 'achha', 'go on', signalling that you are following without interrupting.
Pausing for a few seconds after they finish so they can add what matters most.

cards.title: Listening to Bilal
cards.setting: Video call with Bilal in the Lahore sales office, 11:30 a.m. He has his camera on and a distributor waiting outside.

lines.text: Every launch it is the same. Karachi decides, Karachi forgets, and Lahore takes the insults. Mian sahib from Gulberg called me a liar today.
You feel the urge to defend dispatch. Tariq followed the only list he had. You hold the thought.
And now you people will send me another e-mail with a new process. Twelve distributors, Friday deadline. Can you fix that or not?
(message to you) Before you answer him: what is he really worried about? Find out first.

cards.title: Your first words to an angry Head of Sales
cards.situation: Bilal has just vented for two minutes. He is angry, embarrassed in front of his distributors and suspicious of head office. You know the mistake came from his own ambiguous voice note, and you need accurate facts before you can promise anything. What do you say first?

choices.text: 'You've been embarrassed in front of distributors you've worked hard to win, and Friday is close. Which of the twelve are most at risk, and what did we promise them?'
choices.outcome: Bilal pauses. You reflected his feeling, showed you grasped the deadline and asked an open question. He explains that four large distributors have shelf contracts starting Saturday; the other eight can wait until Tuesday. Now you have something you can actually solve.

choices.text: 'With respect, Bilal sahib, your voice note said ‘usual’. Dispatch did exactly what you asked.'
choices.outcome: Technically true, and it ends the conversation. Bilal hears blame, gets defensive and stops sharing information. You learn nothing about what the distributors actually need.

choices.text: 'Don't worry, I'll get all 3,000 stands to Lahore by Friday, whatever it takes.'
choices.outcome: He calms down for now, but you promised something you have not checked. Tariq later tells you trucks are booked until Thursday. You have turned a listening moment into a broken promise.

choices.text: 'I understand. Please send me an e-mail with all the details and I will look into it.'
choices.outcome: Polite and safe, but Bilal feels brushed off by 'another e-mail'. You eventually get the facts, a day later, with less trust than before.

cards.title: The questioning funnel
cards.caption: Start wide to discover, narrow to understand, then close to confirm. Jumping straight to closed questions makes you miss the real issue.

items.label: Open questions
items.detail: 'What happened with the distributors this morning?' Invite a full answer and reveal the landscape.

items.label: Probing questions
items.detail: 'Which four are most at risk, and why Saturday?' Dig into the details that matter.

items.label: Closed questions
items.detail: 'So if four get stands by Friday and eight by Tuesday, will that work?' Confirm a specific fact or decision.

items.label: Summary and agreement
items.detail: Restate what was agreed, who does what and by when.

cards.back: Cannot be answered with yes or no; usually starts with what, how, tell me or describe. Use it to explore.
Invites a short, specific answer such as yes, no, a number or a date. Use it to confirm facts and close agreements.
A follow-up that digs deeper into something already said: 'What makes Saturday so important?'
Pushes the listener towards the answer you want: 'You agree the plant was careless, don't you?' It produces agreement, not truth.
Explores a possibility: 'What would happen if four distributors got stands on Friday and the rest on Tuesday?'
Mirrors back words or feelings to invite more: 'You said Karachi always forgets?'

cards.question: Mehwish is investigating a late delivery. Which of her questions is a leading question?
options: 'What happened between the truck leaving Hyderabad and arriving in Lahore?'
'How did the driver find out about the road closure?'
'The driver obviously took the long route to claim overtime, didn't he?'
'At what time did the truck reach the Lahore depot?'
cards.explanation: The third question suggests its own answer and pressures the listener to agree, so it is leading. The first two are open, neutral questions and the last is a neutral closed question about a fact.

cards.title: The messages we send without words
cards.body:
Non-verbal and vocal signals carry much of the **emotion** in a message. Key channels:

- **Paralanguage (vocal cues):** tone, pitch, pace, volume, pauses. 'Fine' said flatly is not fine.
- **Kinesics:** facial expressions, gestures, posture, nodding.
- **Eye contact:** shows attention, but norms vary; some staff lower their eyes with seniors as a sign of respect.
- **Proxemics:** use of personal space and distance.
- **Haptics:** touch. In Pakistani workplaces, let a colleague of the opposite gender offer a handshake first; a hand on the heart is a respectful alternative.
- **Chronemics:** use of time, such as punctuality, waiting and reply speed.
- **Appearance and setting:** dress, office layout, who sits where.

When words and signals clash, people usually trust the signals for feelings. Treat any single signal as a **clue to check**, not proof.

cards.title: The 7-38-55 myth
cards.body:
You may have heard that only 7% of meaning is in words, 38% in tone and 55% in body language. That is a misreading. The original laboratory studies looked at **single words expressing feelings or attitudes** where tone and face **contradicted** the word. They never claimed words carry 7% of meaning in a briefing, e-mail or presentation.

The useful lesson is narrower: **when your words and your tone or face send different emotional messages, listeners believe the tone and face.** Keep them consistent, or congruent.

cards.title: Build a closed-loop instruction
cards.prompt: Put the steps of an instruction that cannot be misread into the right order.
steps: State the purpose: why this matters and what success looks like
Give the specifics: what, how many, where, by when and who is responsible
Replace vague words such as 'usual' or 'ASAP' with names, lists and dates
Send it in writing, attaching or linking the exact list or document
Ask the receiver to read back the key points in their own words
Correct any gap, confirm, and agree a check-in point

cards.title: The read-back that saved Friday
cards.body:
That afternoon Tariq rebooks the trucks and receives a new instruction from you in the launch group, with the list attached as a file:

> **Lehar stands, Lahore, urgent.** 1,200 stands to the four distributors on the attached list (tab 'Priority') by Friday 4 p.m. Remaining 1,800 to the other eight by Tuesday. Owner: Tariq. Please read back.

Tariq replies: *'Confirmed: 1,200 to the four on Priority tab by Friday 4 p.m., 1,800 to the rest by Tuesday. Note: Priority tab shows Gulberg twice, so only three distributors?'*

The read-back caught a copying error before a single truck moved. Mehwish fixes the list in ten minutes.

**Why it worked:** purpose, numbers, owner and deadline were explicit; the list was attached, not 'on the drive'; and the receiver restated the meaning, closing the loop.

cards.question: In a review, Tariq says 'No problem, everything is fine', while looking at the floor, speaking quietly and with his arms folded. What is the best response?
options: Accept his words; he is a senior manager and said it is fine
Tell him his body language shows he is lying
Note the mismatch and ask an open question, such as 'What would make this easier for the plant?'
Ignore it, because body language is 55% of meaning and he clearly disagrees
cards.explanation: His words and signals are incongruent, which is a clue worth checking, not proof. An open, non-threatening question invites him to share concerns. Accusing him of lying is unfair, and the 55% claim is a misreading of the research.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Static Room
items: Communication is a loop: sender, encoding, channel, decoding, receiver and feedback, with noise and context affecting every step.
Name the barrier (semantic, psychological, perceptual, physical, cultural, organisational, overload) before choosing a fix.
Active listening means paraphrasing content, reflecting feelings, clarifying and summarising, with purposeful silence.
Use the questioning funnel: open, then probing, then closed to confirm. Avoid leading questions when you need the truth.
Non-verbal signals carry feelings; treat mismatches as clues to check, and keep your own words and tone congruent.
Close the loop on important instructions: specifics, written record and a read-back.

cards.prompt: Think of an instruction you gave or received recently that went wrong. Which part of the communication loop failed, which barrier was involved, and how would a read-back have changed the result?

quiz.question: In the communication model, what is the main purpose of feedback?
options: To let the receiver add new topics and questions to the conversation as it goes along
To repeat the same message through a second channel for emphasis
To show the sender how the message was actually understood
To reduce the amount of noise travelling in the channel
quiz.explanation: Feedback closes the loop: it is the receiver's response that reveals how they decoded the message, so the sender can correct gaps. Repeating through a second channel can help, but it is not feedback.

quiz.question: In communication, what does 'noise' mean?
options: Anything that distorts the intended meaning
Only loud sounds in the physical environment where the communication takes place
Unnecessary or off-topic messages sent in a WhatsApp group
Open disagreement between the sender and the receiver
quiz.explanation: Noise is any interference with meaning: physical noise, but also jargon, stress, assumptions or a poor connection. Limiting it to loud sounds is too narrow.

quiz.question: A new management trainee in a Lahore bank branch is told by the operations officer to 'tag the ECIB hit and park it in the suspense queue'. The trainee nods and does nothing. Which barrier is most likely at work?
options: A physical barrier caused by noise and crowding in the branch
A semantic barrier: unfamiliar jargon and acronyms
An organisational barrier caused by too many management layers between them
A perceptual barrier caused by the trainee's stereotypes about operations staff
quiz.explanation: Unexplained jargon and acronyms are classic semantic barriers: the words arrived but the meaning did not. The trainee's nod also shows anxiety about asking, but the root problem is vocabulary, which plain language would fix.

quiz.question: A customer says, 'I've visited this branch three times and still nobody can tell me why my card is blocked.' Which response reflects the customer's feeling rather than paraphrasing the content?
options: 'So you have come in three times about your blocked card.'
'When did your card first stop working?'
'Let me check your card status right now.'
'You sound really frustrated, and I can understand why.'
quiz.explanation: Reflecting names the emotion you notice, here frustration. Restating 'three times about your blocked card' is paraphrasing the content; the other two are a question and an action.

quiz.question: What is the recommended order of questions in the questioning funnel?
options: Closed to establish the facts, then open to explore, then probing for detail
Probing first, then open questions, then leading questions to agree
Open, probing, then closed to confirm
Leading, then closed, then open to finish on a friendly note
quiz.explanation: The funnel starts wide with open questions, narrows with probing questions and finishes with closed questions to confirm facts and agreements. Starting closed limits what you discover.

quiz.question: An internal auditor wants an honest account of why a cash count was late. Which question is most likely to distort the answer?
options: 'Walk me through exactly what happened in the branch from opening time onwards.'
'What got in the way of starting the count on time?'
'At what time did the count actually begin?'
'You were late because the cashier skipped the procedure, right?'
quiz.explanation: A leading question suggests its own answer and invites agreement rather than truth. The other options are neutral open or closed questions that let the facts emerge.

quiz.question: What is the most accurate lesson from the research behind the popular '7% words, 38% tone, 55% body language' claim?
options: Words carry only 7% of the meaning in any business conversation or meeting
Body language matters more than content, even in e-mails and written reports
Presenters should focus on their gestures rather than on what they actually say
Conflicting tone and face outweigh words when feelings are expressed
quiz.explanation: The original studies tested single words expressing feelings with contradictory tone and facial expressions. They support a narrow lesson about incongruent emotional messages, not a general rule that words carry 7% of meaning.

quiz.question: A pharma distribution manager must tell a depot to recall 400 cartons of a particular batch by 6 p.m. Which approach best prevents misunderstanding?
options: Send a quick voice note so the depot team can hear exactly how urgent the recall is
Call the depot manager and repeat the instruction twice, slowly and clearly
A written instruction with batch, quantity, deadline and owner, plus a read-back
Post the instruction in the regional WhatsApp group so that every depot and manager sees it at once
quiz.explanation: A closed-loop instruction combines explicit specifics, a written record and a read-back that confirms meaning. Repeating or broadcasting the message adds no proof that it was understood.

quiz.question: A manager always keeps junior staff waiting outside her office for twenty minutes, but answers her director's calls instantly. Which non-verbal channel is sending a message here?
options: Chronemics, the use of time
Proxemics, the use of personal space
Haptics, the use of touch
Paralanguage, the use of vocal tone
quiz.explanation: Chronemics covers how people use time, including punctuality, waiting and response speed, all of which signal status and respect. Proxemics concerns physical distance and space.

quiz.question: During a one-to-one, a team member says 'Sure, I can take on the extra territory', but her voice is flat, she avoids eye contact and she sighs. What should her manager do next?
options: Accept the yes, because she agreed verbally and that is what counts
Withdraw the request straight away, because her body language clearly shows that she means no
Ask, 'You're happy to do this, aren't you?' to get a clear answer
Ask an open question about how the extra territory would affect her workload
quiz.explanation: Incongruent signals are a clue to explore, not proof of refusal. An open question invites her real view. Asking 'You're happy to do this, aren't you?' is a leading question, which would press her into the agreement she seems unsure about.

sessions.title: Writing That Gets Read: Plain Language, BLUF, E-mail, WhatsApp and Reports
sessions.summary: Learn to write for busy readers: plain language, the pyramid principle and bottom line up front, e-mail and WhatsApp etiquette that protects people and data, clear numbers in lakh, crore and millions, and short reports that separate findings from recommendations.
objectives: Rewrite wordy business text in plain language with active verbs and concrete words
Structure messages with the bottom line up front and the pyramid principle
Choose To, CC and BCC correctly and write subject lines that state the action and deadline
Apply WhatsApp and voice-note etiquette and keep confidential data off informal channels
Write short reports that separate findings, conclusions and recommendations, with numbers readers cannot misread

cards.title: Two question marks from the CEO
cards.setting: War room, Karachi. Week two. Mehwish is staring at her laptop with her chai going cold.

lines.text: I sent Jamshed sahib a full update on Saturday. Eleven paragraphs. Market research, competitor pricing, cooler specifications, everything.
This is his whole reply: '??'. Just two question marks.
Where in the e-mail did you ask him to approve the PKR 1.8 crore for the coolers?
Paragraph nine. After the cooler specifications. It was all important context!
(WhatsApp to Nasreen, 7:52 a.m.) I have twelve minutes between meetings. What do they need from me and by when?
Four days lost on a decision that takes him one minute. Your mission today: make Kehkashan's writing impossible to misread, starting with this e-mail.

cards.title: Plain language: write for the reader, not the writer

scenes.heading: Know your reader and purpose
scenes.narration: Before you type, answer two questions. Who is reading, and what should they do, decide or know after reading? If you can't say it in one sentence, you are not ready to write.

scenes.heading: Short sentences, familiar words
scenes.narration: Aim for an average of about fifteen to twenty words per sentence, one main idea in each, and everyday words. Write 'use', not 'utilise'. Write 'about', not 'with reference to'.

scenes.heading: Active voice and real verbs
scenes.narration: Active voice names who does what: 'Tariq will ship the coolers on Monday.' Passive voice hides the actor: 'The coolers will be shipped.' And turn hidden verbs back into verbs: 'decide', not 'make a decision'.

scenes.heading: Concrete beats vague
scenes.narration: 'Soon', 'a large amount' and 'ASAP' mean different things to different people. Write 'by Thursday 3 p.m.' and 'PKR 18 million'. Specific words remove guesswork.

scenes.heading: Design for skimming
scenes.narration: Busy readers scan. Use a clear subject line, short paragraphs, headings, bullets and bold for the key ask. Then read it once as your reader would, and cut anything they do not need.

cards.title: The pyramid principle
cards.caption: Start with the answer, then the few arguments that support it, then the evidence. Readers who stop early still get the point.

items.label: The answer or main point
items.detail: Your recommendation, conclusion or request, in one or two sentences.

items.label: Key supporting arguments
items.detail: Usually two to four reasons, grouped so they don't overlap and nothing important is missing.

items.label: Evidence and data
items.detail: Facts, figures, examples and analysis behind each argument; often in attachments.

cards.question: Which opening line best applies bottom line up front for Mehwish's e-mail to the CEO?
options: 'As you know, the ready-to-drink dairy market has grown rapidly over the past three years.'
'Please approve PKR 1.8 crore for 600 coolers by Thursday so they reach stores before launch.'
'I hope this e-mail finds you well. I wanted to share a detailed update on Lehar.'
'Our research team has completed a thorough analysis of cooler options.'
cards.explanation: Bottom line up front means the first line states the request, the amount and the deadline, with the reason in brief. The other openings are background or pleasantries that make the CEO hunt for the ask.

cards.title: BLUF, SCQ and grouping your points
cards.body:
**Bottom line up front (BLUF)** means the first one or two sentences say what you want the reader to know or do: the decision, the request, the deadline.

When a reader needs context before the answer makes sense, use a short **SCQ opening**:
- **Situation:** what the reader already accepts ('Lehar launches on 1 March').
- **Complication:** what has changed or gone wrong ('summer heat will spoil stock in stores without coolers').
- **Question:** what this raises ('how do we protect quality in time?'). Your main point answers it.

Then group the supporting points so they are **mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE)**: no overlaps, no gaps. Three reasons such as cost, timing and risk work well; 'cost', 'money' and 'timing' overlap.

Keep detail in attachments. If the e-mail needs scrolling, ask whether a one-page note plus a call would work better.

items.label: Subject line
items.right: Approval needed by Thu: PKR 1.8 crore for 600 Lehar coolers

items.label: First sentence
items.right: The request, the amount and the deadline

items.label: Structure
items.left: Eleven paragraphs in the order she did the work
items.right: Ask, three reasons, risks, next step

cards.title: Fix the office English
cards.prompt: Match each wordy or unclear phrase to its plain-language fix.

pairs.left: 'Kindly do the needful at the earliest.'
pairs.right: Say exactly what you need and when: 'Please send the signed invoice by 3 p.m. today.'
'Please reply with your comments by Friday.'

pairs.left: 'A decision was taken to postpone the launch.'
pairs.right: Active voice that names the actor: 'The launch committee postponed the launch.'

pairs.left: 'We will conduct an investigation into the delay.'
pairs.right: Turn the hidden verb back into a verb: 'We will investigate the delay.'

pairs.left: 'At this point in time, due to the fact that…'
pairs.right: 'Now, because…'
Replace the vague deadline with a real one: 'Please process this by noon Wednesday.'

cards.title: Write an e-mail that gets a decision
cards.prompt: Put the steps of writing an important e-mail in the most effective order.
steps: Decide the purpose: what should this reader do, decide or know?
Write the bottom line as your first sentence
Group two to four supporting points and move detail into an attachment
Close with a clear ask, owner and deadline
Write a subject line that states the action and the date
Check the To and CC lists, then reread as the reader before sending

cards.title: Midnight in the launch group
cards.setting: The 'Lehar Launch' WhatsApp group: 140 members, including staff, agencies and some distributors. Thursday, 11:40 p.m.

lines.text: (voice note, 3:12) @Tariq sahib, the second shipment is AGAIN short. Every time the plant makes excuses and my team looks stupid in front of the market.
Short because sales changed the order twice yesterday. I have the e-mails. Should I post them here?
Thirty-one people have seen it. Two distributors react with a laughing emoji. Then someone forwards the confidential trade-price sheet 'for reference'.
(to Nasreen) Why are our price sheet and our internal fights in a group with outsiders at midnight?
(to you) You are now an admin of that group. We need rules by tomorrow, and someone needs to calm this down tonight.

cards.title: A public fight in the group
cards.situation: It is almost midnight. Bilal and Tariq are arguing publicly in a 140-member WhatsApp group that includes external distributors. The confidential price sheet has just been forwarded into the group. You are the admin. What do you do first?

choices.text: Reply in the group: 'Both of you please stop. This is unprofessional.'
choices.outcome: The fight pauses, but both senior managers have been publicly scolded in front of distributors. Bilal leaves the group; Tariq stops responding to you for two days. The price sheet is still visible.

choices.text: Message Bilal and Tariq privately and deal with the price sheet in the morning
choices.outcome: Moving the argument private is right, but leaving confidential prices visible overnight to external members lets more people see and save them.

choices.text: Leave it until the morning meeting; nobody reads WhatsApp at midnight
choices.outcome: Thirty-one people had already read it. By morning a distributor has shared the price sheet with a rival brand, and the fight has become office gossip.

choices.text: Delete the price sheet for everyone if you still can, post a neutral note ('Taking this offline; update by noon tomorrow'), and message Bilal and Tariq privately to arrange a call
choices.outcome: The sheet is removed from the chat, the public argument stops without anyone losing face, and the issue moves to a private channel. You also tell Nasreen that the sheet was exposed, because outsiders may already have saved it.

cards.front: Who goes in the To line?
cards.back: People who must act or reply. If you need nothing from someone, they do not belong in To.
People who need to stay informed but are not expected to act. Use it sparingly; every CC adds to someone's inbox.
When e-mailing many external people who should not see each other's addresses. Not for secretly copying your boss on a conversation.
Only when everyone on the thread needs your reply. 'Thanks' or 'Noted' to 200 people wastes 200 people's time.

cards.front: You're furious about an e-mail. Now what?
cards.back: Write the reply if you need to, but don't send it. Wait, reread when calm, or pick up the phone. Angry e-mails get forwarded.

cards.front: Sent something confidential to the wrong people?
cards.back: Contain it fast: recall if your system allows, tell your manager and the data owner at once, and send one short note asking recipients to delete it without forwarding. Never hope nobody noticed.
One topic per e-mail where possible, so the subject line stays accurate and the thread is easy to find and act on.
Read as shouting. Use bold sparingly for the key ask or deadline instead.

cards.title: Is WhatsApp the right channel?
cards.prompt: Sort each message by the most appropriate channel, assuming a typical company policy.
buckets: Needs e-mail or an official system

items.text: 'Reaching the Gulberg office in 15 minutes, start without me'
A quick photo of the Lehar display at a store in Clifton
'Reminder: today's call is at 3 p.m., link below'
Approval of PKR 1.8 crore spending on coolers
A formal warning to an employee about performance
Final agreed terms of a distributor contract
Photos of customers' CNICs collected at a promotion
A colleague's medical report explaining their leave
The confidential trade-price sheet, in a group with outsiders

cards.title: Ten rules for work WhatsApp
cards.body:
- Give every group a **purpose**, an **admin** and pinned rules.
- Keep groups internal unless outsiders truly need them.
- Respect working hours; schedule non-urgent messages.
- **Voice notes:** short, with a one-line text summary. Long ones can't be skimmed or searched.
- Use 'reply' to quote the message you answer.
- No forwards, jokes or politics.
- Never post customer data, CNIC images, salaries, medical or price information.
- Confirm decisions, approvals and numbers by e-mail or in the official system.
- Criticise in private, never in a group.
- 'Seen' is not 'agreed'; ask for an explicit reply.

cards.title: Lakh, crore and millions
cards.caption: Mixed audiences misread big numbers. In formal writing, state one system and add the other in brackets: PKR 1.8 crore (PKR 18 million).

cards.question: Mehwish's budget note says 'PKR 2.5 crore'. Kehkashan's Dubai-based regional finance team uses the international system. How should she write it for them?
options: PKR 2.5 million
PKR 25 million
PKR 250 million
cards.explanation: One crore is ten million, so 2.5 crore is 25 million. Writing 'PKR 2.5 crore (PKR 25 million)' serves both audiences.

cards.title: Shape of a short business report
cards.caption: Readers often read only the first page. Make it carry the answer.

items.label: Title and date
items.detail: Specific: 'Lehar cooler pilot, Karachi: results and recommendation, 14 February'.

items.label: Executive summary
items.detail: Half a page that stands alone: purpose, key findings, conclusion, recommendation and the decision needed. Written last.

items.label: Background and scope
items.detail: Why the report exists, what was examined and what was not.

items.label: Findings
items.detail: What you found: facts and data, without opinion.

items.label: Conclusions
items.detail: What the findings mean.

items.label: Recommendations
items.detail: What should be done, by whom and by when.

items.label: Appendices
items.detail: Detailed data, methods and tables for readers who want them.

cards.title: Findings, conclusions, recommendations
cards.body:
Weak reports blur three different things. Keep them apart:

- **Finding:** an observed fact. 'Stores with coolers sold 38% more Lehar in the four-week pilot.'
- **Conclusion:** your interpretation of the findings. 'Coolers are the main driver of sales in hot weather.'
- **Recommendation:** an action, with owner and timing. 'Place coolers in the top 600 stores before 1 March; owner: Mehwish.'

Each recommendation should trace back to a conclusion, and each conclusion to findings. If a recommendation has no finding behind it, either find the evidence or drop it.

The **executive summary** is not an introduction. It is the whole report in miniature, written last, readable on its own, and it ends with the decision you need.

cards.question: In the cooler pilot report, which sentence is a conclusion rather than a finding or a recommendation?
options: 'Average Lehar sales were 38% higher in stores with coolers.'
'Install coolers in the top 600 stores before 1 March.'
'Spoilage complaints fell from 41 to 6 during the pilot.'
'Temperature control, not shelf position, is the main cause of the sales gap.'
cards.explanation: A conclusion interprets what the facts mean, here identifying the main cause. The sales and complaint figures are findings, and installing coolers is a recommendation.

cards.title: The one-minute version
cards.body:
**Subject:** Approval needed by Thu 15 Feb: PKR 1.8 crore (PKR 18m) for 600 Lehar coolers

Dear Jamshed sahib,

Please approve PKR 1.8 crore for 600 coolers so they reach our top stores before the 1 March launch. Tariq needs a purchase order by Thursday to meet the supplier's lead time.

**Why:**
- **Sales:** pilot stores with coolers sold 38% more Lehar.
- **Quality:** spoilage complaints fell from 41 to 6.
- **Timing:** the next supplier slot is in April, after the launch.

**Risk if we wait:** summer stock spoils in stores and early reviews suffer.

The full pilot report is attached. I can brief you in five minutes at any time today.

Regards,
Mehwish

*Jamshed's reply, four minutes later: 'Approved. Well written.'*

cards.title: Take-aways from the Inkwell
items: Know your reader and purpose before writing; use short sentences, active voice, real verbs and concrete numbers and dates.
Put the bottom line up front, use SCQ when context is needed, and group support so it is MECE.
To is for action, CC for information, BCC for protecting external addresses; reply all only when everyone needs it.
On WhatsApp: purpose, admin, working hours, short voice notes with a text summary, no data or price leaks, criticise in private.
Write big numbers so both systems understand them: 1 crore = 10 million; 10 lakh = 1 million.
Reports separate findings, conclusions and recommendations; the executive summary stands alone and states the decision needed.

cards.prompt: Find the last important e-mail you sent. Could the reader act on it from the subject line and first two sentences alone? Rewrite those lines using bottom line up front.

quiz.question: What does 'bottom line up front' (BLUF) mean in business writing?
options: Put the financial figures at the top of every e-mail and report
Keep the conclusion for the final paragraph so the reader follows the logic
State the main point, request or decision in the first sentence or two
Write the subject line in capitals so it stands out in the inbox
quiz.explanation: BLUF puts the conclusion or request first so a busy reader gets it immediately. Leaving the conclusion to the end is the traditional academic order that BLUF replaces.

quiz.question: According to the pyramid principle, what belongs at the top of a written argument?
options: The detailed data and analysis
The answer or main point
The background and history of the issue
A list of everyone consulted
quiz.explanation: The pyramid starts with the governing answer, supported by a few grouped arguments, which in turn rest on evidence. Data sits at the base, often in attachments.

quiz.question: An operations manager needs the finance controller to approve overtime for the Eid dispatch rush by Wednesday. Which subject line is most effective?
options: Approval needed by Wed: Eid dispatch overtime, PKR 6.5 lakh
Overtime
Some thoughts on the upcoming Eid period and our dispatch team
URGENT!!! PLEASE READ
quiz.explanation: A strong subject line states the action, the topic, the key figure and the deadline, so the reader knows what is needed before opening. Vague or shouting subject lines are skipped or resented.

quiz.question: You need your manager to sign off a vendor payment, and the procurement officer only needs to know it is happening. How should you address the e-mail?
options: Both in To, so neither feels left out
Manager in To, procurement officer in CC
Procurement officer in To and manager in BCC
Manager in CC, procurement officer in To
quiz.explanation: To is for people who must act; CC is for people who need to stay informed. BCC should not be used to hide your manager on a conversation.

quiz.question: When is BCC most appropriate?
options: Secretly copying your manager so a colleague doesn't know they are watching
Copying people who need to act on the e-mail
Any e-mail with more than five recipients inside the company
Sending one invitation to many external guests who should not see each other's addresses
quiz.explanation: BCC protects the privacy of external recipients on large mailings. Using it to copy your boss secretly damages trust if discovered, for example when the boss replies all.

quiz.question: Which rewrite of 'A decision was made by the committee to conduct a review of the pricing' is the clearest?
options: 'It was decided by the committee that a review of pricing would be conducted.'
'A review of the pricing has been decided upon.'
'The committee decided to review the pricing.'
'Pricing review: decision made.'
quiz.explanation: The best rewrite uses active voice (the committee decided) and turns hidden verbs (decision, review) back into verbs. 'It was decided by the committee...' keeps the passive voice, and 'A review has been decided upon' hides who decided.

quiz.question: You need to update your regional manager, who is between client visits, on three issues at a Rawalpindi depot. What is the best WhatsApp approach?
options: A four-minute voice note explaining the full background of each issue
Three separate voice notes, one for each issue, so she can listen in order
A forwarded chain of the depot team's messages so she sees everything first-hand
A short text with the three issues as numbered lines and what you need from her
quiz.explanation: A busy reader needs something she can skim in seconds and refer back to. Long voice notes cannot be skimmed or searched, and forwarded chains make her do the summarising.

quiz.question: Which statement about the executive summary of a report is correct?
options: It stands alone, is written last and states the recommendation and decision needed
It should introduce the topic and context, and leave all of the findings and conclusions for the main body of the report
It is written first, to guide the structure of the rest of the report
It should list every finding in detail so nothing is missed
quiz.explanation: The executive summary is the whole report in miniature, written once you know your conclusions, and it must make sense on its own. Treating it as an introduction is the most common mistake.

quiz.question: A Lahore client quotes a project budget of 'PKR 45 lakh'. How should you write this for a foreign head office that uses the international system?
options: PKR 45 million
PKR 0.45 million
PKR 4.5 million
quiz.explanation: One lakh is 100,000, so 45 lakh is 4,500,000, or 4.5 million. PKR 45 million would be 4.5 crore.

quiz.question: In a 60-member team WhatsApp group, a supervisor posts: 'Ahmed, your report was full of errors AGAIN. Fix it.' As the group admin and Ahmed's manager, what is the best response?
options: Reply in the group to defend Ahmed's work so the team sees fairness
Message the supervisor privately about criticising in public, and check on Ahmed separately
Remove the supervisor from the group immediately
Ignore it; the comment was about work, not about Ahmed as a person
quiz.explanation: Criticism belongs in private. Addressing the supervisor privately corrects the behaviour without a second public clash, and checking on Ahmed deals with the impact. A public defence escalates the argument.

sessions.title: Presenting With Confidence: Structure, Story, Slides, Nerves and Q&A
sessions.summary: Plan presentations around one key message, structure them so audiences follow and act, use stories and clean slides, turn nerves into energy and handle tough questions calmly, including from a hostile room.
objectives: Analyse the audience and state a presentation's key message in one sentence
Structure a talk with a hook, roadmap, three main points, summary and call to action, and plan the time
Tell a short business story with a character, a complication and a resolution that proves your point
Design slides with headline titles, one idea each and minimal text
Manage nerves and handle questions, including hostile, confidential and unanswerable ones

cards.title: Thirty-four slides and twelve minutes
cards.setting: A hotel ballroom on M.M. Alam Road, Lahore. Three days before the Lehar distributor conference. Mehwish is rehearsing to an empty room.

lines.text: Two hundred and twenty distributors. Twelve minutes. Thirty-four slides. I'll just have to talk fast.
Talk fast and they will talk louder. And Mian sahib from Gulberg will ask about margins in front of everyone. He enjoys it.
Last time I presented, my voice shook so much I read the slides word for word. People were on their phones by slide five.
Then let's not fix your voice first. Tell me in one sentence: what should a distributor think or do when you finish?
Umm... understand the full Lehar marketing plan, the pricing, the cooler programme, the trade schemes and the research?
That's five sentences. Your mission for this stage: help Mehwish find one, and get her ready for Mian sahib.

cards.title: Plan before you open the slides

scenes.heading: Who is in the room?
scenes.narration: Start with the audience. What do they already know, what do they care about, what worries them, and what language are they most comfortable in? Distributors care about margin, stock turnover and support, not about our research methods.

scenes.heading: Why are you speaking?
scenes.narration: Decide whether you mainly want to inform, persuade or inspire. Then write the action you want: 'Distributors sign up for the cooler programme before they leave the hall.'

scenes.heading: One key message
scenes.narration: Write your key message as one sentence a listener could repeat to a colleague. 'Lehar sells faster than anything else in the chiller, and we pay for the chiller.' If you can't, you are not ready to build slides.

scenes.heading: Fit the time
scenes.narration: Most presenters speak at around 120 to 150 words a minute. Plan for about 130, and fill only about 90 percent of your slot, because introductions, pauses and technical hiccups always eat time.

scenes.heading: Then, and only then, slides
scenes.narration: Sketch the story on paper first: opening, three main points, close. Slides come last, as support for the speaker, not as a script.

cards.title: A structure audiences can follow
cards.caption: Tell them where you are going, take them there, then remind them where they have been. Plan your final words for after the questions.

items.label: Hook
items.detail: A story, a striking number or a question that earns attention in the first 30 seconds.

items.label: Why it matters to them
items.detail: Connect the topic to the audience's own goals or problems.

items.label: Roadmap
items.detail: 'Three things today: the product, the support, the money.'

items.label: Three main points
items.detail: Each with evidence, an example or a story. Three is easy to remember.

items.label: Summary and call to action
items.detail: Restate the key message and the exact action you want.

items.label: Questions
items.detail: Take questions while you still have time in hand.

items.label: Final close
items.detail: End on your key message, not on the last random question.

cards.question: Which of these is the strongest key message for Mehwish's distributor presentation?
options: 'Today I will cover the Lehar marketing plan, pricing, coolers, trade schemes and research.'
'Lehar is an exciting new product for Kehkashan Foods.'
'Lehar sells faster than anything else in the chiller, and Kehkashan pays for the chiller.'
'Please ask questions at any time during the presentation.'
cards.explanation: A key message is one memorable sentence that matters to the audience and leads to action. The first option is an agenda, not a message, and the second is too vague to change anyone's mind.

cards.title: Planning numbers for a 12-minute slot
cards.caption: Planning figures, not rules. Rehearse aloud with a timer to find your own pace.

items.label: Words per minute
items.detail: A comfortable planning pace; most presenters fall between about 120 and 150.

items.label: Of the slot to fill
items.detail: Leave the rest for pauses, introductions and surprises. For 12 minutes, plan about 10.8.

items.label: Words of script
items.detail: 10.8 minutes × 130 words ≈ 1,400 words, about three typed pages, not five.

items.label: Main points
items.detail: Audiences remember three ideas far more easily than seven.

cards.title: Stories make the point stick
cards.body:
Data persuades the head; a story makes people care and remember. A good business story is **short (about a minute)**, **true** and has four parts:

1. **Situation:** a real person and place. 'Razia baji runs a small general store in Ichhra.'
2. **Complication:** a problem or conflict. 'Every summer her lassi spoiled within two days, so she stopped stocking it.'
3. **Resolution:** what changed. 'In our pilot she got a Lehar cooler. She sold out every three days.'
4. **Point:** link it to your message. 'That's what the chiller programme does for you.'

Use specific, sensory details: names, places, numbers. Pair the story with one strong number so it is not dismissed as a one-off. Get permission before using a real customer's story, or change identifying details.

cards.title: Build the Razia story
cards.prompt: Put the parts of Mehwish's opening story in the most effective order.
steps: Razia baji runs a small general store in Ichhra, Lahore
Every summer her lassi spoiled within two days, so she stopped stocking it
In the pilot she received a Lehar cooler, paid for by Kehkashan
She now sells out every three days and asks for more stock
Across the 40 pilot stores, cooler outlets sold 38% more
That is what the chiller programme can do for every one of you

cards.title: Document slides versus presentation slides
cards.caption: If your slides make sense without you, they are a document. Send the document; present with slides.

items.label: Title
items.right: A headline sentence: 'You earn more per shelf with Lehar'

items.label: Content
items.right: One idea, one visual or a few words

items.label: Text size
items.right: Large enough to read at the back (24pt or more as a guide)

cards.title: Helps or hurts the audience?
cards.prompt: Sort each slide habit by its effect on a live audience.

items.text: A slide title that states the takeaway as a full sentence
One chart with the key bar in colour and the rest in grey
A black screen while you tell a story
High contrast text such as dark on light
Reading every bullet aloud word for word
A full spreadsheet pasted as an image
Thirty-four slides for a twelve-minute talk
Animations flying in for every bullet

cards.title: Why reading slides fails
cards.body:
People read faster than you speak, and they cannot read one thing while listening to something different. When you put full sentences on a slide, the audience reads ahead, stops listening and then waits for you to catch up.

So: **few words on screen, your words in the air.** Keep detailed numbers for a handout or the follow-up e-mail. If a slide needs a lot of text, such as legal terms, pause and let people read it in silence.

cards.title: The shaking hands
cards.setting: Rehearsal, the night before. The deck is now 9 slides. Mehwish's hands are trembling on the clicker.

lines.text: The slides are better. But my heart is pounding and I haven't even started. What if I freeze?
At the plant we say: the machine shakes before it runs smoothly. Nobody fires the operator for that.
Your body is giving you energy. Our job is to aim it. First, your opening: can you say the first thirty seconds without notes?
Not yet. And what do I do when Mian sahib attacks the margin?

cards.back: Myth. Most experienced speakers still feel nerves. They have learned to use the energy and not to fight it.

cards.front: The audience can see how nervous you are.
cards.back: Usually far less than you think. Most of what you feel inside, such as a racing heart, is invisible from the seats.

cards.front: Fastest way to calm the body?
cards.back: Slow breathing, with the out-breath longer than the in-breath, for a minute or two before you start.
Not enough. Rehearse out loud, standing, with a timer, ideally in front of one or two colleagues.
Nerves peak at the start. A well-practised opening carries you until your body settles.

cards.front: Should you tell yourself to calm down?
cards.back: Calling the feeling excitement, 'I'm ready for this', often helps more than trying to force calm.

cards.front: What to do on the day?
cards.back: Arrive early, test the projector, clicker and microphone, and chat with a few audience members so the room feels friendlier.

cards.question: Ten minutes before going on stage, Mehwish feels her heart racing. Which action is most likely to help?
options: Reading through all nine slides one last time on her phone
Drinking a strong coffee for extra energy
Telling herself firmly not to be nervous
Slow breathing with a longer out-breath, then running through her memorised opening
cards.explanation: Slow breathing with a longer exhale calms the body, and a rehearsed opening carries her through the moment when nerves peak. Last-minute rereading tends to raise anxiety, and trying to force calm rarely works.

cards.title: Answering any question
cards.caption: The same loop works for friendly, tough and hostile questions.

items.label: Listen to the end
items.detail: Don't interrupt or start answering in your head. Notice the concern behind the words.

items.label: Pause
items.detail: A two-second pause shows you are taking the question seriously and gives you time to think.

items.label: Rephrase
items.detail: Repeat it so the whole room hears it, and remove any loaded or hostile wording.

items.label: Answer briefly
items.detail: Answer to the whole room, not just the questioner. Facts first, then one example.

items.label: Bridge back
items.detail: Link the answer to your key message, then check: 'Does that answer your question?'

cards.title: Mian sahib stands up
cards.situation: Conference day. Mehwish has finished her talk. Mian sahib stands at the back: 'Madam, this is a nice show, but your margin is two percent lower than the other brands in my chiller. Why should I give you my shelf? Are you taking us for fools?' The room goes quiet. What should she do?

choices.text: 'Sir, nobody is taking anyone for a fool. Our margin is competitive if you look properly at the numbers.'
choices.outcome: She repeats his insult and implies he hasn't read the numbers. The room takes his side, and the argument moves to whether she was rude.

choices.text: Pause, then: 'The question is whether Lehar earns you more per shelf despite a lower margin per bottle. In the pilot it sold almost twice as fast...' and offer to go through his figures afterwards
choices.outcome: By rephrasing, she removes the insult and turns the question into one she can answer with evidence. Turnover beats margin per bottle, and the offer of a one-to-one shows respect. Several distributors nod. Mian sahib sits down: 'Theek hai, show me after.'

choices.text: 'That's a good question. Let me take it offline with you after the session.'
choices.outcome: Polite, but the whole room heard the challenge and nobody heard an answer. Other distributors now suspect the margin story is weak.

choices.text: Invite Bilal to answer, since he knows Mian sahib better
choices.outcome: Bilal answers well, but the audience notices that the presenter could not handle the question on her own. Her credibility on the rest of the plan drops.

cards.title: Tricky questions, steady answers
cards.prompt: Match each Q&A situation to the best way of handling it.

pairs.right: Say so honestly and commit to a specific follow-up: 'I'll confirm the exact figure to you by Thursday.'
Thank them politely, pick out the actual question, answer it briefly.
Acknowledge it, park it and offer to discuss it afterwards.
Note them, then answer them one at a time, starting with the most important.
Rephrase it neutrally before answering; never repeat the insult.
Say clearly that you can't share it and why, then offer what you can share.

cards.question: Why should a presenter repeat or rephrase a question before answering it in a large room?
options: It shows the questioner that the presenter is in charge
So everyone hears the question and any hostile wording is removed
It gives the presenter time to look at the slides for the answer
It is a formality that shows good manners
cards.explanation: Many people in a large room cannot hear a question from the floor. Rephrasing makes it audible and lets the presenter remove loaded wording before answering. It also buys a moment to think, but that is a side benefit.

cards.title: Delivery in five habits
cards.body:
- **Eye contact:** in a big room, divide it into sections and give each thought to one person in a different section.
- **Pause** after a key number or point. Silence gives it weight and replaces 'umm' and 'basically'.
- **Vary your voice:** slow down for important points, and lift your volume at the back of the room.
- **Move with purpose:** stand still when making a key point; move when you change topic.
- **If nobody asks a question,** start it yourself: 'A question I'm often asked is...'

cards.title: Mehwish's first 30 seconds
cards.body:
*(Lights dim. A single photo of a small Lahore shop appears. No title.)*

'Razia baji runs a small store in Ichhra. Every summer, her lassi spoiled in two days. So she stopped stocking it. *(pause)*

This summer, she sold out every three days. *(pause)*

What changed? A cooler. And we paid for it. *(pause)*

Today I'll show you three things: why Lehar moves faster than anything else in your chiller, how the cooler programme works, and what you earn per shelf. By the end I'll ask you to sign up for coolers before you leave this hall.'

**What it does:** a real story hooks the room, the pauses let it land, the roadmap gives three points, and the call to action is stated up front. The distributors look up from their phones.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Spotlight Hall
items: Start with the audience and the action you want; write your key message as one sentence before making any slides.
Structure: hook, why it matters, roadmap, three points, summary and call to action, questions, then a planned final close.
Plan about 130 words a minute and fill about 90% of the slot.
Tell short true stories: situation, complication, resolution, point, backed by one strong number.
Slides support the speaker: headline titles, one idea each, few words, highlighted takeaways.
Use nerves as energy: slow breathing, rehearse aloud, memorise the opening. In Q&A: listen, pause, rephrase, answer briefly, bridge back.

cards.prompt: Think of your next presentation or team briefing. Write its key message in one sentence, the action you want from the audience, and the one question you most fear. How will you rephrase and answer it?

quiz.question: What is the best test of whether you are ready to start building slides?
options: You have collected all the data and research available on the topic, ready to paste in
You can state your key message in one sentence a listener could repeat
You have chosen the slide template and colour scheme your audience will see
You know exactly how many slides your manager expects you to show
quiz.explanation: If you cannot say your key message in one sentence, more slides will not fix it. Data, templates and slide counts come after you know what you want the audience to think and do.

quiz.question: You have a 10-minute slot at a sales conference. Using the course's planning figures (about 130 words a minute, filling about 90% of the slot), roughly how many words should your script be?
options: About 1,170 words
About 1,300 words
About 1,500 words
About 900 words
quiz.explanation: 90% of 10 minutes is 9 minutes, and 9 × 130 = 1,170 words. Using the full 10 minutes gives 1,300 words, which leaves no buffer for pauses or delays.

quiz.question: Which slide title best supports a live presentation?
options: 'Cooler outlets sold 38% more Lehar in the pilot'
'Pilot results'
'Sales data: Q1, by store type, with and without coolers'
'Slide 7 of 9'
quiz.explanation: A headline title states the takeaway as a sentence, so the audience knows what the slide proves even if they glance at it for a second. Topic titles make them work it out.

quiz.question: At a town-hall meeting, an employee asks the HR head: 'Why does management keep hiding the bonus formula from us?' What should the HR head do before answering?
options: Say firmly and clearly that management is not hiding anything from employees
Ask the employee to explain exactly what he means by 'hiding'
Rephrase it neutrally: 'The question is how the bonus formula works and is shared'
Repeat the question word for word, exactly as it was asked, so that everyone in the hall hears it
quiz.explanation: Rephrasing lets the whole room hear the question while removing the loaded word 'hiding', so the answer can focus on facts. Repeating it word for word amplifies the accusation; denying it argues with the framing.

quiz.question: A board member asks a presenter for a figure she does not have to hand. What is the best response?
options: Give her best estimate confidently, as if it were the confirmed number, to avoid looking unprepared
Say she doesn't have it and commit to sending it by a specific time
Move on quickly to the next question so the gap isn't noticed
Explain at length why the figure is so hard to calculate
quiz.explanation: Honesty plus a specific follow-up protects credibility. A guess presented as fact can be quoted back later and damage trust far more than 'I'll confirm by Thursday'.

quiz.question: Which technique is most effective for calming physical nerves just before presenting?
options: Slow breathing, with the out-breath longer than the in-breath
Holding your breath for as long as possible to slow your heart
Rereading all of your slides one final time on your phone
Telling yourself firmly to stop being nervous
quiz.explanation: Slow breathing with a longer exhale helps settle a racing heart. Last-minute rereading usually raises anxiety, and ordering yourself to be calm rarely works.

quiz.question: A trainer wants to open a safety session with a story. Which order follows the business-story structure taught in this session?
options: A named worker; the shortcut that injured him; the guard now fitted; why every guard matters
Why every guard matters; the guard that is now fitted; the injury; and finally the worker's name
Industry injury statistics; a list of the safety rules; then a short anecdote at the very end
The worker's name; why every guard matters; the guard now fitted; the shortcut
quiz.explanation: The structure is situation (a real person and place), complication (the problem), resolution (what changed) and point (the link to the message). Starting with statistics or the moral loses the story's power.

quiz.question: Why should a presenter plan a short final close to deliver after the question-and-answer session?
options: Because questions should only be taken once the closing remarks are finished
So the presenter can correct any mistakes made in their answers
Because organisers expect speakers to use every minute of the slot
So the audience leaves with the key message, not the last random question
quiz.explanation: If the session ends on a stray or hostile question, that becomes what people remember. A planned closing line after Q&A restates the key message and the call to action.

quiz.question: A finance manager has a 10-minute slot to present budget variances to the leadership team. Her draft has 28 dense slides. What is the best advice?
options: Pick the three variances that matter most, one headline slide each, and send detail as a pre-read
Keep all 28 slides but speak noticeably faster so that every variance and every number still gets covered in the slot
Reduce the font size so each slide holds more numbers
Present the 28 slides and skip any that get no questions
quiz.explanation: A live audience can follow a few ideas well, not 28 slides of detail. Leading with the most important points and moving detail to a pre-read respects both the time and the content.

quiz.question: Presenting to 300 people in a large hall, how should a speaker manage eye contact?
options: Keep looking at the most senior person in the front row, since they matter most
Look slightly above everyone's heads at the back wall of the hall
Give each thought to one person, moving between sections of the room
Look mainly at the slides so the audience follows them
quiz.explanation: Delivering each thought to one person in a different section makes the whole room feel included. Staring at one VIP or the back wall disconnects you from most of the audience.

sessions.title: Meetings, Feedback and Difficult Conversations
sessions.summary: Turn expensive, circular meetings into short sessions that decide things, record decisions and actions properly, give and receive feedback with a situation-behaviour-impact approach and handle difficult conversations assertively, not aggressively or passively.
objectives: Calculate the cost of a meeting and decide whether a meeting is needed at all
Write agendas with outcomes, owners and timings, and facilitate so every voice is heard and decisions are made
Record minutes that capture decisions and actions with owners and deadlines
Give and receive feedback using situation, behaviour and impact, privately and promptly
Plan and hold difficult conversations assertively using a describe-express-specify-consequences structure

cards.title: The meeting that never ends
cards.setting: Week five. The Monday launch meeting, Karachi board room, with Lahore and Hyderabad on the screen. Eighteen people. Hour two.

lines.text: Good news first: 160 of the 220 distributors signed up for coolers after Mehwish's talk. Bad news: demand now outruns supply, and the Monday meeting has become a battlefield.
My team has orders for 40,000 cases. The plant sends 25,000 and tells us to be grateful. Every week the same story!
Every week you change the forecast. You want me to run the lines on guesswork? Let me finish my...
Tariq sahib, with respect, your plant always has an excuse.
(to you, in the chat) No agenda, no decisions, and the cooler roll-out item hasn't even come up. Third week running.
From next Monday, you chair this meeting. And somebody needs to talk to Bilal about how he treats Tariq. I think that somebody is you.

cards.title: What the Monday meeting really costs
cards.caption: Meeting cost ≈ attendees × hours × average hourly cost. The PKR 2,500 an hour average loaded cost here is an assumption for Kehkashan; use your own organisation's figure.

items.label: People in the room
items.detail: Including six who attend 'just in case' and speak once.

items.label: Length
items.detail: Booked for one hour, regularly running to two.

items.label: Cost per meeting
items.detail: 18 × 2 × PKR 2,500, before counting lost selling and plant time.

items.label: Decisions recorded
items.detail: In the last three meetings, according to the notes.

scenes.heading: Does this need a meeting?
scenes.narration: Meetings are for things that need live discussion: decisions, solving problems, and building agreement. Pure updates can go in an e-mail or a shared tracker. If nothing needs discussing, cancel the meeting and give people their time back.

scenes.heading: Purpose and outcome
scenes.narration: State the purpose and the outcome you want: 'By 11 a.m. we will have agreed the Lahore allocation for March.' An outcome tells everyone when the meeting has succeeded.

scenes.heading: Only the right people
scenes.narration: Invite those who must decide, those with essential information and those who must carry out the result. Others can read the minutes.

scenes.heading: Agenda and pre-reads
scenes.narration: Send the agenda and any pre-reads a day or two in advance. Each item gets an owner, a time and its outcome type: decide, discuss or inform. Then nobody spends the meeting reading figures for the first time.

scenes.heading: Clear roles
scenes.narration: A chair or facilitator steers the discussion, a timekeeper watches the clock and a note-taker records decisions and actions. In small meetings one person may take two roles, but every role must be covered.

cards.title: Two agendas for the same Monday

items.label: Heading
items.right: Launch meeting: agree March allocation and cooler roll-out

items.label: Item 2
items.right: DECIDE: Lahore allocation for March (Tariq, 20 min)

items.label: Pre-reads
items.right: Sales and capacity figures, sent Friday

items.label: Attendees
items.right: Eight people who decide or deliver

cards.question: Which agenda item is written most effectively?
options: 'Plant issues'
'Coolers: discussion'
'Any other business'
'DECIDE: Lahore allocation for March. Owner: Tariq. 20 minutes. Pre-read: capacity sheet'
cards.explanation: A strong agenda item states the outcome type, the topic, an owner, a time and any pre-read. Vague labels such as 'Plant issues' invite open-ended arguments with no clear end point.

cards.title: Decide, discuss or just inform?
cards.prompt: Sort each item for next Monday by the outcome it needs.

items.text: Choose between the two cooler suppliers' final offers
Approve the revised Lahore allocation for March
Ideas for Ramadan in-store activity
Risks the plant sees in running a third shift
Last week's sales figures by city
The new travel claim form
HR's confirmed dates for the Eid holidays

cards.title: Facilitation: steering without dominating
cards.body:
A good chair keeps the meeting on purpose and makes sure the best thinking, not the loudest voice, wins.

- **Start and end on time.** Review the action log first.
- **Agree ground rules:** one conversation at a time, phones down, challenge ideas not people.
- **State the decision rule upfront:** will the chair decide after hearing views, will the group seek consensus, or will it vote?
- **Use a parking lot:** note off-topic issues on a visible list and agree when they will be handled.
- **Bring in quiet voices:** a round-robin ('Let's hear from each site'), or ask directly by name with a real question.
- **Ideas first, silently:** ask everyone to write ideas for two minutes before discussing, so the first voice doesn't anchor the group; the most senior speaks last.
- **Manage dominators:** thank, summarise and redirect: 'Got it, Bilal. Tariq, your view?'
- **Summarise each item:** what was decided, who does what, by when.

cards.title: The chair's toolkit
cards.prompt: Match each meeting problem to the facilitation technique that fixes it.

pairs.left: An important but off-topic issue derails the discussion
pairs.right: Note it in the parking lot and agree when and where it will be handled.

pairs.left: The Hyderabad team never speaks on the video call
pairs.right: Run a round-robin, or invite them by name with a specific question.

pairs.left: The most senior person's idea always wins
pairs.right: Collect ideas silently in writing first, then discuss them.

pairs.left: People argue for 30 minutes about who decides
pairs.right: State the decision rule at the start of the item.
Review the action log at the start of every meeting.

pairs.left: One person keeps talking over others
pairs.right: Thank, summarise their point and redirect to someone else.

cards.title: The meeting cycle
cards.caption: The meeting itself is only one step. Most of the value comes from what happens before and after.

items.label: Plan
items.detail: Purpose, outcome, people and whether a meeting is needed at all.

items.label: Prepare
items.detail: Agenda with owners and times; pre-reads sent a day or two ahead.

items.label: Run
items.detail: Roles, ground rules, facilitation and summaries of each item.

items.label: Record
items.detail: Minutes with decisions and actions, circulated within 24 hours.

items.label: Follow up
items.detail: Owners deliver; the action log opens the next meeting.

cards.title: Minutes that drive action
cards.body:
**Lehar launch meeting, Monday 3 Feb, 10:00–10:45**
Present: Nasreen, Bilal, Tariq, Mehwish, you (chair), plus three others. Notes: Ali.

**Decisions**
1. Lahore March allocation set at 32,000 cases; the balance goes to Islamabad.
2. Cooler supplier: Option B, subject to a 30-day warranty.

**Actions**
| What | Who | By |
|---|---|---|
| Confirm revised allocation to Lahore distributors | Bilal | Wed 5 Feb, 5 p.m. |
| Costing for a third shift | Tariq | Fri 7 Feb |
| Supplier warranty in writing | Mehwish | Thu 6 Feb |

**Parking lot:** sales incentive rules, at the next HR review.

Note what is missing: no record of who said what. Minutes capture **decisions, actions (what, who, by when) and essential context**, not a transcript.

cards.question: Which action item from a meeting is recorded most usefully?
options: 'Allocation to be looked into.'
'Tariq: confirm third-shift costing to Nasreen by Friday 7 Feb.'
'Plant team will try to improve supply soon.'
'Everyone to follow up on distributor concerns.'
cards.explanation: A usable action names one owner, a specific task and a deadline. The others hide the owner, use passive voice or give the task to 'everyone', which in practice means no one.

cards.title: After the meeting
cards.setting: Corridor outside the board room. The new format worked: 45 minutes, two decisions. But Bilal interrupted Tariq six times and called the plant 'lazy'.

lines.text: I'm not coming to these any more. I'll send my numbers by e-mail. I don't need to be insulted in front of juniors.
If Tariq stops coming, the allocation decisions fall apart. Bilal needs to hear the impact of what he does. Today, while it's fresh.
(passing) Good meeting! Finally something got decided. See, a bit of pressure works.
Bilal is senior to you and thinks the meeting went brilliantly. How do you tell him?

cards.title: Situation, behaviour, impact: a feedback path
cards.caption: Describe what you saw, not what you think the person is. Then listen.

items.label: Situation
items.detail: When and where: 'In this morning's launch meeting, during the allocation item...'

items.label: Behaviour
